cse-2005-cs-68.approach: Draw the 5-stage timing with operand forwarding: a load's value is available after MA, so the dependent ALU instruction stalls one cycle; the next ALU instruction gets $I_2$'s result forwarded EX→EX with no stall.

steps.title: I1 (load)
steps.body: IF1 RD2 EX3 MA4 WB5 — R0 is available at the end of MA (cycle 4).

steps.title: I2 depends on I1
steps.body: I2 needs R0 in its EX; earliest is cycle 5 (forward MA→EX). So IF2 RD3 stall4 EX5 MA6 WB7.

steps.title: I3 depends on I2
steps.body: I3 needs the new R0 from I2's EX (cycle 5) → EX in cycle 6 via EX→EX forwarding. It was held one cycle by the stall ahead of it: IF3 stall4 RD5 EX6 MA7 WB8.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Last WB in cycle 8 → **8 clock cycles**. (Without forwarding the count would be 11 or 13, neither of which is an option, confirming forwarding is assumed.)

optionAnalysis.reason: 5 cycles for $I_1$ + 1 load-use stall + 1 + 1 for the next two instructions = 8.
10 would mean extra stalls between $I_2$ and $I_3$, which forwarding removes.
12 is close to the no-forwarding count, not supported by any consistent timing.
15 is fully sequential execution ($3\times5$), ignoring pipelining.

pitfalls: Forgetting the unavoidable one-cycle load-use stall even with forwarding (gives 7, not an option).

cse-2005-cs-69.approach: In program-controlled (busy-wait) mode the CPU is tied up for the whole inter-byte gap; in interrupt mode it spends only the interrupt overhead per byte. Gain = gap / overhead.

steps.title: Time per byte
steps.body: $10\text{ KB/s} \Rightarrow 10^4$ bytes/s $\Rightarrow$ one byte every $\frac{1}{10^4}\text{ s} = 100\ \mu s$.

steps.title: CPU time per byte
steps.body: Programmed I/O: the CPU polls for the full $100\ \mu s$. Interrupt mode: only $4\ \mu s$ (transfer time negligible).
